title: Databases in tests
summary: Test EF Core queries against a real relational engine: SQLite in memory with an open connection, why the EF InMemory provider misleads, Testcontainers for the production database, and keeping tests independent of each other's data.

steps.title: Which database does a test talk to?
body: A query is only tested when SQL actually runs it. The common choices, from fastest to most faithful:
| Option | What it is | Catches | Misses |

| EF Core **InMemory** provider | a dictionary pretending to be a database | almost nothing about SQL | translation errors, constraints, transactions, case sensitivity. Microsoft's docs advise against it for testing |
| **SQLite in memory** | a real SQL engine in your process | translation, constraints, ordering, most query bugs | provider differences (PostgreSQL's types, collations, `ILIKE`, JSON columns) |
| **Testcontainers** | the real PostgreSQL/SQL Server in a throwaway Docker container | everything, migrations included | needs Docker; seconds to start, so share one container per collection |
SQLite in memory lives as long as its **connection** is open, so keep one connection per test and hand it to EF:

With Testcontainers the shape is a collection fixture (`IAsyncLifetime`) that starts `new PostgreSqlBuilder().Build()` once, applies migrations, and gives each test a clean state (a transaction rolled back at the end, or Respawn to clear tables).

steps.prompt: A query uses `.Where(c => c.Email == email)`. Tests on the EF InMemory provider pass, but production on SQL Server finds `Ada@Example.com` when searching for `ada@example.com`. What does this show?
options: The InMemory provider compares with C# rules (case-sensitive) while the real database uses its collation (case-insensitive by default on SQL Server): only a real engine shows real behaviour
The test should use `ToLower()` on both sides
InMemory tests must run in parallel
steps.explain: Collation, NULL semantics, constraints and translation all live in the database. Test queries on a relational engine; for anything provider-specific, use the production engine in a container.

steps.prompt: Match each need to the approach.
pairs: fast tests for LINQ queries and constraints
SQLite in memory with an open connection
each test starts from empty tables in a shared container
a transaction rolled back after each test, or Respawn
the database disappears between two `DbContext` instances
keep one `SqliteConnection` open and pass it to `UseSqlite`

steps.title: Test the overdue-invoice queries on SQLite
prompt: The billing queries, compiled beside your tests (EF Core with SQLite is available in this step):
// Unpaid invoices due before today, oldest first.
public static List<Invoice> Overdue(BillingDb db, DateOnly today) =>
// What one customer still owes, in cents.
public static long Owed(BillingDb db, string customer) =>
Write `public class BillingTests : IDisposable` with a fresh SQLite in-memory database per test (see the card), seed the invoices each test needs, and write at least **4** tests. Five planted bugs.
solution: void Seed(params Invoice[] invoices) { db.Invoices.AddRange(invoices); db.SaveChanges(); db.ChangeTracker.Clear(); }
static Invoice Inv(string customer, int dueInDays, long cents, bool paid = false) =>
new() { Customer = customer, Due = Today.AddDays(dueInDays), AmountCents = cents, Paid = paid };
Seed(Inv("ada", -3, 100), Inv("ada", 5, 250), Inv("ada", -9, 999, paid: true), Inv("bob", -1, 400));

target: public static List<Invoice> Overdue(BillingDb db, DateOnly today) =>
public static long Owed(BillingDb db, string customer) =>

hints: A small helper keeps seeding readable: `Seed(params Invoice[] invoices)` that adds, saves, and clears the change tracker so queries really hit the database.
Order needs at least two overdue invoices whose due order differs from their insert order.
For `Owed`, seed another customer and a paid invoice for the same customer, and assert the exact cents.
steps.explain: Every query ran as real SQL on SQLite: the `DateOnly` comparison, the ordering and the `SUM`. A fresh in-memory database per test means no test can see another's data, in any order.
